title: Olympiad Day 10: Uzbekistan in command as medal race goes to the wire
summary: India, Ukraine, Germany and Hungary remain in contention after a dramatic penultimate round The medal race has been dramatically reshaped going into the final round. Uzbekistan strengthened its position with a commanding 3.5–0.5 victory over Armenia, while India matched that score against Uzbekistan 2 but remains a full match point behind the hosts. In the Women’s section, Mongolia’s medal hopes suffered a major blow after a 3–1 defeat to Poland, while Vietnam continued their impressive late surge with a fourth consecutive match win, edging Indonesia 2.5–1.5 to keep an outside medal chance alive. Full results 46th Chess Olympiad Let’s take a closer look at the action from the playing hall. Ceremonial moves mark a historic day in Samarkand At the start of the round, Principal Arbiter Ivan Syrovy announced that Timur Turlov had just won the FIDE presidential elections, celebrated at the nearby Congress Center, becoming the eighth FIDE President. In the second round of voting, Turlov received 110 votes against 85 for his opponent, Wadim Rosenstein. Following the announcement, Syrovy gave way to the ceremonial moves. Shaikh Khaled Al Qasimi, President of the Arab Chess Federation and Chairman of the Sharjah Sports Council, opened the game with 1.e4 for Armenia’s first board, Haik Martirosyan. Hussein Abdullah Al-Khoury, Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Chess Club and Tournament Director of the 47th FIDE Chess Olympiad in the UAE, replied with the solid 1…c6 for Uzbekistan’s Nodirbek Abdusattorov, who subsequently changed his move and opted for the surprising Scandinavian Defence instead. The action then moved a few boards towards the women’s section, where Khakimov Akbar, Director of the “Afruza” Chess Club, played 1.e4 for Afruza Khamdamova in the Uzbekistan–Peru match. Open section Uzbekistan takes control in key Armenia match Javokhir Sindarov won the first game of the key match between Uzbekistan and Armenia, defeating Robert Hovhannisyan with a very nice piece of home preparation that featured an exchange sacrifice. Immediately afterwards, his second during the Candidates, Mukhiddin Madaminov, brought home Uzbekistan’s second win against Gabriel Sargissian on board four, again displaying some astonishing tactical play. After the game, Sindarov gave an interview sharing his thoughts on the match and was joined towards the end by Madaminov. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eIaHaHLknfk A final victory by Nodirbek Abdusattorov in a long ending on board one completed an outstanding 3.5–0.5 victory for Uzbekistan, putting the hosts in prime position to fight for gold tomorrow. Abdusattorov is playing the best chess of his life so far: undefeated and on an impressive 8/10. India keeps the pressure on Uzbekistan The second important match of the round brought India up against Uzbekistan 2, the revelation team of the event. A big favourite on paper, India showed that they remain serious contenders right up until the final game of the tournament. Nihal Sarin opened the scoring for India on board three, defeating Mukhammadzokhid Suyarov with the black pieces. Sarin accepted two sacrificed pawns from his opponent before doubling down on the defense and eventually reeling in the full point. After a solid draw on board two, World Champion Gukesh D prevailed in a tactical ending against Ortik Nigmatov on board four, securing the match victory for India. Praggnanandhaa then added another win on board one to complete the 3.5–0.5 scoreline. The result leaves Uzbekistan one full match point ahead of India going into the final round, with a substantial 30-point advantage on the tiebreak. Ukraine shock China to keep medal hope alive China came into the round in a unique position in the medal race. All they needed was to avoid defeat against 12th seeds Ukraine, a team that had fought its way back into contention by winning its last three matches. But it was not to be. Igor Kovalenko scored an important point on board one by defeating former World Champion Ding Liren, who unexpectedly dropped an exchange after a long period of manoeuvring. Position of the day Igor Kovalenko – Ding Liren The two players had been shuffling their pieces for around 20 moves, each waiting for a positional improvement or a mistake from the opponent. White emerged slightly better: Black has more weaknesses, while his bishop pair is hardly active. Instead of natural 44…Rd8 or 44…Qd7, keeping the ball rolling, Ding Liren blundered with 44…Re6? which failed to 45.Ne3! The queen is attacked, and Black cannot avoid losing the exchange. Following 45…Qf7 46.Ng5 White forked the queen and rook. It was the kind of mistake one simply does not expect from a player of Ding Liren’s strength, but it also demonstrated once again that even the very best players can go wrong at any moment. With boards two and three ending in draws, Ukraine sealed the match with a second victory on board four, where current European Champion and teenage star Roman Dehtiarov defeated Xiangrui Kong. Ukraine now has a real opportunity to fight for a medal if they can produce another victory in the final round. Germany and Hungary stay in medal race Germany will also have a chance to fight for a medal in the final round after a convincing 3–1 victory over France. Hungary matched that score against Spain, keeping both teams firmly in contention heading into the decisive final round. Round 11 pairings: Open Women’s Section China keeps the lead with a tie against India In the match of the day, China and India traded wins on the two lower boards, with Vantika Agrawal suffering her first loss against Lu Miaoyi, undefeated on an impressive 8.5/10. Meanwhile, Savitha Shri raised her remarkable score to 8.5/9 by defeating Zhai Mo. Kazakhstan just one point behind The result allowed China to retain the lead, but their advantage over Kazakhstan was reduced to just one match point. Kazakhstan defeated France 2.5–1.5 in an unbelievable finish. title: Inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards celebrate the people and achievements shaping chess worldwide
summary: The inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards were presented in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, bringing together the global chess community to celebrate outstanding achievements both on and off the board during the 2024–2026 Olympiad cycle. Held alongside the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, the ceremony honoured leading players, teams, tournaments, federations, creators and initiatives whose work has contributed to the development and global reach of chess. Established in 2026 as a biennial programme, the FIDE Excellence Awards cover achievements from September 2024 to August 2026. Following an open nomination process, ten nominees in each of the 11 categories were shortlisted by the FIDE Excellence Awards Jury before the final recipients were determined by the FIDE Excellence Awards Panel. The evening began with welcoming remarks from Odil Abdurakhmanov, representative of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan for Sports, who highlighted Uzbekistan’s role as a crossroads of cultures and civilizations and spoke about chess as something that reaches far beyond sporting competition – a universal language capable of bringing people together. Viswanathan Anand then welcomed the guests and thanked the Government of Uzbekistan for its hospitality and for hosting the event in Samarkand. Reflecting on the purpose of the awards, Anand stressed that the success of chess is built not only by its champions, but by a much wider community. “Behind every great player, there are people who supported them, directly or indirectly: federations, coaches, arbiters, organizers, sponsors, promoters, photographers, professionals from many backgrounds who use chess as a tool to help people grow and become better,” Anand said. “Tonight is about recognizing them and their efforts. The Excellence Awards are an opportunity to bring some of those achievements into the spotlight and simply say thank you. Thank you for being there when it mattered, thank you for providing support when it was important, and for seeing an opportunity that others did not,” he added. Anand concluded by congratulating all nominees and recipients and extending FIDE’s gratitude to everyone contributing to the game, whether recognised during the ceremony or not. Excellence on and around the board The awards programme in Samarkand celebrated achievements across different areas of the chess world, from emerging talent and remarkable sporting returns to team success, inclusion, content creation, tournaments and social initiatives. Yağız Kaan Erdoğmuş was named Best Breakthrough (Rookie of the Year), recognising the extraordinary rise of one of the world’s leading young talents. Levon Aronian received the Best Comeback award, following another remarkable chapter in his long career at the highest level. The Best Team award went to India’s Open and Women’s National Teams, recognising an exceptional period for Indian chess, highlighted by the historic double gold at the 2024 Chess Olympiad in Budapest and a series of major international successes. Łukasz Nowak was named Best Chess Player with a Disability, with Łukasz Turlej accepting the award on his behalf. Remembering Daniel Naroditsky A particularly meaningful moment of the evening came with the presentation of the Daniel Naroditsky Best Creator Award. The category carries the name of the late American grandmaster, educator, commentator and content creator Daniel Naroditsky, honouring his exceptional ability to share chess knowledge and bring the game closer to audiences around the world. Before announcing the recipient, Arkady Dvorkovich paid tribute to Naroditsky and his contribution to the chess community. “He made an amazing contribution to promoting chess to younger generations and to everyone who loved the spirit of chess. He worked endlessly, and he was the kind of person who was loved by everyone.” Dvorkovich described preserving Naroditsky’s legacy as something carrying both institutional and personal significance before announcing ChessBase India as the first recipient of the Daniel Naroditsky Best Creator Award. As part of the recognition, the winner also receives a free spot at the next Naroditsky Memorial in Charlotte, further connecting the award with the tournament established to celebrate Naroditsky’s life and legacy. Excellence beyond the board The ceremony continued by recognising tournaments, organisations and initiatives whose impact extends across the international chess community. The Qatar Masters Open received first place in the Best Tournament (Open) category, followed by the Grenke Freestyle Chess Open in second place and the Sharjah Masters in third. In the Best Tournament (Round Robin) category, Norway Chess took first place, with the Sinquefield Cup second and the Cairns Cup third. Among the developments recognised at Norway Chess was the establishment of its women’s tournament with an equal prize fund. In the Best Federation category, the Uzbekistan Chess Federation received first place, with the Kazakhstan Chess Federation taking second and the All India Chess Federation third. The award recognised the work of national federations in developing chess, supporting players and strengthening the game at both grassroots and elite levels. The awards also celebrated projects using chess to create a broader social impact. Chess in Schools and Communities received first place for Best Chess Initiative, followed by Chess for Freedom in second and The Gift of Chess in third. Special recognition The evening also included special recognition for the Bundesliga, honouring one of the world’s most established and prestigious national chess leagues. The FIDE America Social Initiatives Program 2025 was also recognised for its work across the continent. Implemented through the CCA Diversity Commission, the programme supported 14 completed initiatives across 11 countries, demonstrating how chess can be used to promote inclusion and social engagement in different communities. The Best Chess Player (Female) and Best Chess Player (Male) awards will be presented separately during the Closing Ceremony of the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, completing the inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards programme. With the final awards of the Gala presented, the inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards evening came to a close in Samarkand, celebrating the players, teams, organisers, creators, federations and initiatives whose achievements and contributions continue to shape chess around the world. Written by Angelika Valkova Photos: KNZO Photography

title: DGT hosts two e-Board Operator Seminars at 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand
summary: DGT, the leading designer, developer, manufacturer, and distributor of chess-related products, held two seminars alongside the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Led by Frans Peeters, the seminars brought together 46 participants from 33 countries and territories. Each session took place over two mornings, during which attendees had the opportunity to learn how to set up and run a chess tournament using DGT e-Boards and LiveChess. Participants also gained hands-on experience with the equipment, putting their newly acquired knowledge into practice. The attendees were highly eager to learn and had many questions for the instructor, Frans Peeters. The strong interest in DGT technology from participants worldwide was evident throughout the sessions. At the end of the seminar, each participant received a gift bag containing various DGT merchandise items and a certificate recognising them as a DGT e-Board Operator. The seminars concluded successfully, equipping a new group of experts with the tools to bring chess tournaments to life online. The full list of participants can be found HERE.

title: Timur Turlov elected President of FIDE
summary: Timur Turlov, President of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, was elected President of the International Chess Federation (FIDE). The elections were held on 26 September at the FIDE General Assembly, alongside the 46th Chess Olympiad, in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Turlov won in the second round, with 110 votes. At 38, he becomes the second youngest FIDE President ever elected. Delegates representing 196 national chess federations took part in the election, with three candidates competing in the race. In the first round, Turlov received 96 votes, Wadim Rosenstein (Germany) received 76 votes, and Jan Henric Buettner (Germany) received 20 votes. In total, 192 votes were cast. In the second round, which followed two hours later, Turlov won by a vote of 110 to 85 (196 votes in total), becoming the eighth President of FIDE. He succeeded Arkady Dvorkovich, who served two terms as President, from 2018 to 2026. “We are all one family, and we will continue working as one. This is a great responsibility and a vote for a better future of our sport,” Timur Turlov said following the result. “I am grateful to everyone who supported my campaign and to everyone who took part in this election. We may have different opinions, but we all share one belief – that chess is important and that we can do much more to develop it around the world by making our Member Federations stronger and more independent,” he added. “I look forward to moving chess forward and giving the game the spotlight it deserves,” Turlov concluded. In his congratulations to Timur Turlov, former FIDE President Arkady Dvorkovich wished him success in his work. “Timur has already done a great deal for chess, and I am sure he will do even more now as FIDE President. He and his team have the energy, a clear plan, and resources to deliver and this election result shows Timur has significant backing. We are all one family, and we all share the same goal – for chess to be bigger, better and stronger in the world,” Dvorkovich said. Abdulla Aripov, Prime Minister of Uzbekistan, host of both the 46th FIDE Olympiad and the FIDE Congress, greeted those attending and noted the country’s commitment to promoting chess and friendship in the world. Biography: Timur Turlov Timur Turlov (born on 13 November 1987) is an economist and serves as the Chief Executive Officer of Freedom Holding Corp., an international financial services group listed on the NASDAQ Stock Exchange, with a capitalisation of nearly $11 billion. Since January 2023, he has served as President of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation. Turlov is also the founding President of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF), established in September 2024. Playing chess since childhood, Turlov – a father of six – has supported chess tournaments in Kazakhstan and abroad. Over three years, Freedom Holding Corp. allocated approximately $30 million to the development of chess in Kazakhstan and supported the staging of more than 20 major international FIDE tournaments, becoming one of the largest private sponsors of the game worldwide.  In September 2024, together with FIDE, Turlov initiated the founding of the International School Chess Federation and serves as its President. With a strong belief in the value of education and the role of chess in personal and professional development, the ISCF works with schools, educational organisations, NGOs and national federations to expand chess in education and promote the game among young people worldwide.   He chairs the Turkic Chess Association, which brings together the national chess federations of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Türkiye and Uzbekistan. Under the Association’s auspices, the inaugural Turkic Countries Team Chess Championship was held in Astana in 2026.  With a deep connection to chess tradition and a strong belief in innovation, Timur Turlov advocates the use of digital solutions to help FIDE and national federations advance modern, transparent and sustainable governance, improve services and provide more effective support for players and chess communities around the world.
